_comment: Metaphysics levels 9-11: evil as privation, natural theology/Five Ways, preambles vs mysteries of faith

questions.prompt: Classical metaphysics holds that goodness is convertible with being -- everything that exists is good in some real respect. Given this, how does classical metaphysics actually understand evil?
choices: A real privation -- a lack of a good a thing ought to have, not a positive substance in its own right
As a positive substance existing in its own right, equal and opposite to goodness
As simply an illusion, with no real bearing on anything that actually happens
As something that exists independently of goodness, with no real relationship to it at all
questions.correctAnswer: A real privation -- a lack of a good a thing ought to have, not a positive substance in its own right
questions.explanation: If everything that exists is good in some real respect, evil cannot be a positive thing existing in its own right -- it must be a real privation, a real lack of a good a thing actually ought to have, existing only as a real absence within something that is itself still fundamentally good.
questions.hint: Recall the previous level's own real teaching that goodness is convertible with being -- consider what this implies about anything claiming to be purely, positively evil.

citations.quote: God looked at everything he had made, and found it very good.

questions.prompt: True or False: Calling evil a 'real privation' means it has no real, practical effect on anyone -- as if it were make-believe.
questions.explanation: False, and this is a real, important distinction -- a privation is not the same as nothing at all. Blindness is a real privation of sight, not the same as never having had eyes -- it has real, painful, practical effects, even though it is metaphysically an absence rather than a positive substance.
questions.hint: Consider blindness as an example -- is it 'nothing at all,' or a real, painful absence of something a person ought to have?

citations.quote: God looked at everything he had made, and found it very good.

questions.prompt: Why does the real distinction 'privation, not substance' actually matter for how the Church answers the classical problem of evil -- if God is all-good and all-powerful, why does evil exist?
choices: God never made evil directly -- it enters through a real lack, sin, or a real defect
Because it means evil does not actually exist in any real sense at all
Because it means God is, in fact, equally the real author of both good and evil
Because it has no real bearing on the classical problem of evil whatsoever
questions.correctAnswer: God never made evil directly -- it enters through a real lack, sin, or a real defect
questions.explanation: This is exactly why the real distinction matters -- if evil were a positive substance, God would have had to create it directly, which would contradict his own perfect goodness. As a real privation, evil enters only through a real, created lack, never as something God himself positively made.
questions.hint: Consider what would follow for God's own goodness if evil actually were a positive substance he had to create.

citations.quote: God looked at everything he had made, and found it very good.

questions.prompt: True or False: This level's own real teaching on evil as privation connects directly to this app's own Dogmas-and-doctrine topic, which already taught that God permits evil out of respect for real creaturely freedom, without ever being its real cause.
questions.explanation: True, and naming this direct connection matters -- Dogmas-and-doctrine's own earlier real teaching (God is never the real cause of moral evil) and this level's own metaphysical explanation (evil as real privation, not substance) are two real sides of the very same coherent answer.
questions.hint: Recall this app's own Dogmas-and-doctrine topic, and its own earlier real teaching on God's relationship to evil.

citations.quote: God looked at everything he had made, and found it very good.

questions.prompt: A skeptic objects: 'Calling evil a mere 'absence' trivializes real horrors like cruelty and suffering -- as if evil weren't actually serious.' What is the real, careful answer?
choices: Calling evil a privation says nothing about its real seriousness -- a severe privation can be devastatingly real
The objection is correct, and this metaphysical account should simply be abandoned
Evil is not actually serious at all, precisely because it is metaphysically a privation
This level's own real account has no real answer to this specific real objection
questions.correctAnswer: Calling evil a privation says nothing about its real seriousness -- a severe privation can be devastatingly real
questions.explanation: This objection confuses a metaphysical claim (what kind of thing evil is) with a moral or practical claim (how serious it is). A privation can be devastatingly real and serious in its actual effects -- the metaphysical account explains evil's real structure, without ever minimizing its real, lived weight.
questions.hint: Consider whether 'privation' as a metaphysical category actually says anything about how painful or serious a given evil is.

questions.prompt: Aquinas' 'Five Ways' are five philosophical arguments for:
choices: The existence of God, reasoned from effects observable in the world
The number of angels in each choir
The date of Christ's return
The correct calendar for Easter
questions.correctAnswer: The existence of God, reasoned from effects observable in the world
questions.explanation: From motion, causation, contingency, degrees of perfection, and the order of nature, Aquinas argues that reason alone, reflecting on the world, can conclude that God exists -- prior to and apart from revelation.
questions.hint: Each of the five starts from something we can observe in the world around us.

citations.quote: converging and convincing arguments, which allow us to attain certainty about the truth
God, the source and end of all things, can be known with certainty from the consideration of created things, by the natural power of human reason

questions.prompt: True or False: The First Vatican Council solemnly taught that the existence of God cannot be known with certainty by reason alone, only by faith.
questions.explanation: Vatican I taught the opposite: God 'can be known with certainty from the created world by the natural light of human reason.' Faith is still needed to know the mysteries of the Trinity and Incarnation, but not for God's bare existence.
questions.hint: Vatican I's teaching runs the other direction from this statement.

citations.quote: God, the source and end of all things, can be known with certainty from the consideration of created things, by the natural power of human reason
God, the first principle and last end of all things, can be known with certainty from the created world by the natural light of human reason.

questions.prompt: Romans chapter 1 teaches that God's 'eternal power and divine nature' have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, through the things that have been ____.
questions.explanation: St. Paul argues that creation itself, rightly reasoned about, leaves people without excuse for failing to recognize God's existence -- a foundational scriptural basis for natural theology.
questions.hint: It's the created things themselves that reveal the Creator.

citations.quote: Ever since the creation of the world, his invisible attributes of eternal power and divinity have been able to be understood and perceived in what he has made. As a result, they have no excuse

questions.prompt: The 'argument from contingency' reasons that since everything in the world could have failed to exist (is contingent), there must ultimately be something that:
choices: Exists necessarily, not depending on anything else for its existence
Also could have failed to exist, just like everything else
Is the largest thing in the universe
Was created a very long time ago
questions.correctAnswer: Exists necessarily, not depending on anything else for its existence
questions.explanation: If every single thing merely could exist or not, an infinite chain of merely-possible things could never get started on its own. Something must exist necessarily, in itself, to ground the existence of everything contingent.
questions.hint: An endless chain of 'maybe it exists, maybe it doesn't' can't explain itself.

citations.quote: God, the source and end of all things, can be known with certainty from the consideration of created things, by the natural power of human reason

questions.prompt: True or False: Because natural theology can establish God's existence through reason alone, the Church considers divine revelation of mysteries like the Trinity and the Incarnation unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Reason can reach God's existence and some of his attributes, but the inner life of the Trinity and the Incarnation are truths reason could never discover on its own -- they depend entirely on God freely revealing himself.
questions.hint: Natural theology gets reason to God's doorstep -- it doesn't get inside the house on its own.

citations.quote: The Trinity is a mystery of faith in the strict sense, one of the 'mysteries that are hidden in God, which can never be known unless they are revealed by God'.

questions.prompt: Match each term in natural theology to its meaning.

pairs.right: Knowledge of God available to unaided human reason
Knowledge of God that depends on God's own self-disclosure
Aquinas' philosophical arguments for God's existence
Vatican I's teaching that God can be known with certainty by reason

questions.explanation: Natural and revealed theology are not competitors -- reason can establish that God exists and something of what he is like, while revelation alone discloses who God is in himself, as Trinity and as Christ Incarnate.
questions.hint: Two of these are broad categories of theology; two are specific arguments or documents.

citations.quote: God, the source and end of all things, can be known with certainty from the consideration of created things, by the natural power of human reason
God, the first principle and last end of all things, can be known with certainty from the created world by the natural light of human reason.

questions.prompt: What do the Five Ways actually conclude to, and what do they not?
choices: Each ends at something 'all call God' — an unmoved mover, a necessary being — not at the Trinity, which is known only by revelation
They demonstrate the Trinity philosophically
They prove the God of the Bible in every detail
They establish only that belief in God is permissible
questions.correctAnswer: Each ends at something 'all call God' — an unmoved mover, a necessary being — not at the Trinity, which is known only by revelation
questions.explanation: Overstating the conclusion is the commonest way these arguments are misused. They reach a first cause and no further; that this cause is Father, Son and Spirit is revealed, not deduced. Claiming more invites the fair reply that the arguments have not delivered it.
questions.hint: Ask what a purely philosophical argument could establish about a mystery known only by revelation.

questions.prompt: True or False: Since reason can reach God's existence, the Church holds that revelation about God is unnecessary.
questions.explanation: False, and Vatican I taught both halves. Reason can attain God's existence in principle; revelation remains morally necessary so that these truths can be known by everyone, readily, with firm certainty and without admixture of error. In principle attainable and in practice reliably attained are different claims.
questions.hint: Distinguish what reason can do in principle from what people actually manage without help.

questions.prompt: The argument from contingency reasons that if everything were contingent, there would be nothing now; so there must be something ____ — existing of itself.
questions.explanation: A contingent thing has existence received rather than owned. If every existing thing were like that, existence would have to come from somewhere else at every point and never actually be grounded. The argument is about a present dependency, not about a first event long ago.
questions.hint: The contrast term for contingent is not 'eternal' but something stronger.

questions.prompt: Match each claim in natural theology to its precise scope.

pairs.right: Taught by Vatican I as attainable in principle
So the truth is known by all, readily and without error
Conclude to a first cause, not to the Trinity
Two wings, neither reducible to the other

questions.explanation: The Church's position is a narrow path between rationalism, which makes revelation redundant, and fideism, which makes reason irrelevant. Dei Filius condemned both, and each of these four claims is doing work to hold that line.
questions.hint: Two of these guard against rationalism and two against fideism.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: The previous level named what the Five Ways conclude to and what they do not. Theology gives a precise name to truths reason alone can reach, like God's real existence. What is that name?
choices: Preambles of faith -- truths reason can establish on its own, which faith then builds further upon
Mysteries of faith -- truths reason could never discover on its own, even in principle
Private revelations -- truths revealed only to particular individuals
Disciplinary rules -- changeable regulations with no real philosophical content
questions.correctAnswer: Preambles of faith -- truths reason can establish on its own, which faith then builds further upon
questions.explanation: Theology distinguishes 'preambles of faith' (like God's existence, reachable by reason alone) from the deeper 'mysteries of faith' (like the Trinity, which reason could never discover on its own, even in principle) -- the Five Ways reach only the first real category.
questions.hint: Recall the previous level's own real distinction between what the Five Ways conclude to, and what they do not.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Trinity, which this topic's own earlier level called a real mystery of faith, is a preamble of faith reason alone could have discovered.
questions.explanation: False. The Trinity is precisely the opposite real case -- a genuine mystery of faith, something reason alone could never have discovered, only known because God himself has revealed it.
questions.hint: Recall this topic's own earlier level on the Trinity as a real mystery of faith.

citations.quote: The Trinity is a mystery of faith in the strict sense, one of the 'mysteries that are hidden in God, which can never be known unless they are revealed by God'.

questions.prompt: Given this real distinction, why does philosophy's own real reach -- as far as it goes -- still matter for a believer's faith, rather than being religiously beside the point?
choices: Establishing the preambles first gives real footing under the deeper mysteries revelation adds
Because philosophy's own real reach actually has no bearing whatsoever on genuine religious faith
Because philosophy can, in fact, fully prove every mystery of faith on its own, making revelation strictly unnecessary
Because the preambles of faith are considered more important than the mysteries of faith themselves
questions.correctAnswer: Establishing the preambles first gives real footing under the deeper mysteries revelation adds
questions.explanation: This is the real, positive point of naming this distinction -- philosophy's real reach is not religiously irrelevant just because it falls short of the deepest mysteries; it gives real, rational footing under everything revelation then builds further upon.
questions.hint: Consider what real, practical difference it makes for faith to have some rational footing under it, even before revelation adds anything further.

questions.prompt: True or False: This app's own Dogmas-and-doctrine topic already relied on this same real distinction when it taught that God's oneness can be known by reason, while the Trinity requires revelation.
questions.explanation: True. Dogmas-and-doctrine's own earlier levels already applied exactly this real distinction -- God's existence and oneness as a preamble reason can reach, the Trinity as a mystery revelation alone provides -- this level simply names that same real distinction with its own precise theological vocabulary.
questions.hint: Recall this app's own Dogmas-and-doctrine topic's earlier levels on God's oneness and on the Trinity.

citations.quote: The Trinity is a mystery of faith in the strict sense, one of the 'mysteries that are hidden in God, which can never be known unless they are revealed by God'.

questions.prompt: A skeptic objects: 'If reason can only reach the preambles, philosophy's real contribution to faith is actually pretty minor.' What is the real, careful answer?
choices: A real foundation isn't minor -- it's what everything else is built on, supporting revelation, not competing with it
The objection is correct, and philosophy's real contribution to faith should simply be dismissed as unimportant
Philosophy's real contribution to faith is, in fact, larger than revelation's own contribution
Reason and revelation actually compete for the exact same real ground, with one having to lose for the other to matter
questions.correctAnswer: A real foundation isn't minor -- it's what everything else is built on, supporting revelation, not competing with it
questions.explanation: This objection treats 'foundation' as if it meant 'minor.' In fact, a real, secure foundation is exactly what makes everything built on top of it possible -- philosophy's real contribution is foundational, not competing with revelation, but genuinely supporting it.
questions.hint: Consider whether a foundation is actually a minor part of a building, or the part everything else depends on.

questions.prompt: True or False: This level's own real distinction -- preambles versus mysteries -- is simply a restatement of this topic's very first level, on what metaphysics itself actually asks.
questions.explanation: False, though the two are genuinely related -- this topic's first level distinguished metaphysics from physics; this level distinguishes what reason alone can reach from what only revelation adds, a real, further distinction built on, not identical to, the first.
questions.hint: Recall this topic's very first level, and consider whether it actually made this same specific real distinction.
